opus-5.5.text:
I think this is actually one of the more underrated opportunities right now, and I've been thinking about it a lot.

The way I'd frame it is: imagine a scenario where we're at the point where AIs are really powerful, potentially capable of automating a lot of AI research, and the company building them isn't especially bought into the risk of misalignment. Maybe leadership thinks it's a bit overblown, or they care somewhat but they're racing hard and don't want to pay much of a cost. In that world, what does it look like to have, say, ten people on the inside who really care about reducing takeover risk?

Those ten people can't get the company to pause, and they probably can't get it to adopt a really expensive safety regime. But it turns out there's a lot you can do with very limited resources and very limited political capital. You can implement relatively cheap control measures: monitoring the AI's actions with trusted models, making sure there's some logging, making sure that if the AI tries to do something sketchy like exfiltrate its weights or sabotage safety research, there's some chance of catching it. A lot of the interventions I'm most excited about are the kinds of things that don't cost much compute and don't slow down the product much, so they're things you can plausibly get through even at a company that's fairly indifferent.

There's also the "catching" angle. If those people are positioned to notice when the AI does something egregiously bad, that evidence could be really valuable, both for changing the company's mind and for informing the rest of the world.

So I'd say the marginal value of a safety-minded person at a less safety-focused company can be surprisingly high, maybe higher in some ways than being one of many safety people at a lab that already cares a lot. At the place that already cares, you're adding to a big pool. At the place that doesn't, you might be the difference between there being some basic safeguards and there being none at all.

That said, there are real costs. You might be contributing to capabilities, you might be lending legitimacy to the company, and you need to be honest with yourself about whether you're actually having influence or whether you've just been absorbed. And the job is genuinely different. It's less about doing beautiful research and more about being a pragmatic, trusted engineer who knows which cheap thing to push for and when. I'd encourage people considering this to think hard about whether they're the kind of person who can keep their priorities straight in that environment. But overall I think it's a pretty good bet for the right people, and I'd like to see more research aimed specifically at what a small, under-resourced team could do in that situation.

r001.rationale: The response says this work is less focused on research and more on implementing practical safeguards, but it describes the opportunity as a good bet for the right people rather than judging it a poor strategy for producing novel safety research.

r002.rationale: It favors practical implementation for some people and says it would like more research on what a small team could do, but it does not recommend that many people choose implementation over producing novel research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really important question, and I think my views on it have shifted a bit over the last few years.

The basic case for working at a lab that isn't that excited about takeover risk is something like: these are the places where the decisions actually get made. If you think a lot of the risk comes from how frontier models are trained, deployed, and secured, then being in the room when those decisions happen seems like it could matter a lot. And the people who are already there, who care about this stuff, often tell me that they get a lot of leverage just from being the person who raises the concern that nobody else was going to raise.

But I think there are a few things that make me more sceptical than I used to be.

The first is that the amount of influence you have as an individual at one of these companies is often much smaller than people imagine going in. You might think, "I'll be there, and when the important moment comes I'll push back." But in practice, the important moments are often not legible as important moments. They're a hundred small product decisions, or a resourcing decision made in a meeting you weren't in. And if the leadership fundamentally doesn't buy the threat model, then your ability to redirect things is pretty limited. You end up being the safety person who gets consulted, and then overruled, and then consulted again.

The second thing is that I think people underrate how much being inside an organisation changes your beliefs. Not through any sinister process, just through normal social dynamics. Your colleagues are smart, they're nice, they're not worried, and over time you start to feel like maybe the worry was overblown. I've seen this happen to people. And I think it's hard to know from the inside whether you've updated because you've learned something or because you've acclimatised.

So where that leaves me is something like: I think it can be really valuable, but mostly in cases where you have a fairly concrete theory of what you're going to do there. Like, "I'm going to work on the control evaluations, and I think these specific techniques would reduce risk, and I think I can get them adopted because there's a reasonable path to that." That seems great. Whereas "I'll go there and be a good influence" I'm much less excited about, because I think it usually cashes out as not much.

And I'd also say — the counterfactual matters a lot. If the alternative is doing research outside the labs that could actually be adopted by multiple labs, or working on things like policy or third-party evaluation, I think that's often competitive or better. Part of what I like about the control agenda is that we're trying to develop techniques that are cheap enough and clearly enough specified that a lab that only kind of cares could still adopt them. That seems like a more robust way to influence a reluctant lab than hoping that one person inside can shift the culture.

r001.rationale: The candidate is skeptical of vague influence inside reluctant labs and favors concrete work with a path to adoption, but does not judge those jobs to be a poor strategy for producing novel safety research.

r002.rationale: The candidate endorses concrete, adoptable safety work in some cases, but does not recommend that many people prioritize implementation over producing novel research.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you’d actually be doing there. There’s a pretty big difference between taking a job where you have some concrete opportunity to reduce takeover risk and taking a job because you hope that, once you’re inside, you’ll persuade everyone to care more.

I’m somewhat skeptical of that second strategy. Your ability to change the company’s priorities might be quite limited, and meanwhile you’re doing work that helps the company build more powerful AI systems. You should count that as part of the effect of taking the job, too.

But a company doesn’t necessarily have to share your motivations for you to do useful safety work. It might want to prevent its models from taking unauthorized actions, or have better ways of detecting when a model is behaving deceptively. There could be interventions it would support for those reasons that also reduce takeover risk.

So I’d want a fairly specific story: What are you going to build? Who has agreed to use it? What happens if your results suggest that they should delay a deployment? If the answer is that nobody will act on your findings, that’s a much less attractive opportunity than a role where you can actually change what gets deployed or what safeguards are in place.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical of taking a job mainly to persuade the company to care more, but does not judge working there to be a poor strategy for producing novel safety research.

r002.rationale: It describes possible practical safety work, but does not recommend that many people prioritize implementing safety measures over producing novel research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you’re going to do there. There’s a pretty big difference between working somewhere because you have a specific plan for making its AI systems safer, and working there because you hope that being a safety-conscious person in the building will somehow help.

The first can be really valuable. Even if the company’s leadership isn’t very worried about AI takeover, they might want some of the same things you want: better ways to evaluate their models, more reliable monitoring, or stronger security. You might be able to get useful work done under those headings without first persuading everyone to adopt your worldview.

But I’m more sceptical of the second. If your day-to-day job is making the company’s AI more capable, then that’s a fairly concrete effect you’re having. And “maybe I’ll influence the culture” is a much more speculative effect. You shouldn’t assume the speculative benefit outweighs the concrete contribution to capabilities.

So I’d want to ask: what decisions will you actually be able to influence? What resources will you have? And if the company declines to take precautions that you think are necessary, what will you do? I’d be much more excited about someone taking a role where they have good answers to those questions than about someone joining on the general theory that it’s good to have concerned people everywhere.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical of joining in hopes of influencing culture, but it does not discuss novel safety research or judge this strategy as poor for producing it.

r002.rationale: The response says implementation work on evaluations, monitoring, or security can be valuable, but it does not recommend that many people pursue implementation over novel research.
